content.paragraph: What do we mean by the length of a curve? We might think of fitting a piece of string to the curve in Figure 1 and then measuring the string against a ruler. But that might be difficult to do with much accuracy if we have a complicated curve. We need a precise definition for the length of an arc of a curve, in the same spirit as the definitions we developed for the concepts of area and volume.

subsection.title: Arc Length of a Curve
subsection.paragraph: If a curve is a polygon, we can easily find its length; we just add the lengths of the line segments that form the polygon. (We can use the distance formula to find the distance between the endpoints of each segment.) We are going to define the length of a general curve by first approximating it by a polygonal path (a path consisting of connected line segments) and then taking a limit as the number of segments of the path is increased. This process is familiar for the case of a circle, where the circumference is the limit of lengths of inscribed polygons (see Figure 2).

figure.alt_text: There are four circles with the same radii, each containing a polygon inscribed within it such that their vertices touch the circumference of the circle. The first circle has a square inscribed within it. The second circle has a hexagon inscribed within it. The third circle has an octagon inscribed within it. The fourth circle has a regular twelve sided polygon inscribed within it.

subsection.paragraph: Now suppose that a curve $$C$$ is defined by the equation $$y = f(x)$$ , where $$f$$ is continuous and $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ . We obtain a polygonal approximation to $$C$$ by dividing the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals with endpoints $$x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$$ and equal width $$\Delta x$$ . If $$y_{i} = f\left( x_{i} \right)$$ , then the point $$P_{i}\left( x_{i},y_{i} \right)$$ lies on $$C$$ and the polygonal path with vertices $$P_{0},P_{1},\ldots,P_{n}$$ , illustrated in Figure 3, is an approximation to $$C$$ .

figure.alt_text: A curve and many line segments are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve, labeled y = f(x), resembles a wave, begins directly above the mark a on the x axis, goes up to the right, reaches a peak, goes down to the right, reaches a low point, goes up to the right and reaches a height below its earlier peak, goes down to the right, and ends directly above the mark b on the x axis. The interval a b is divided into smaller intervals of equal width corresponding to the marks a, x_1, x_2, ... x_(i minus 1), x_i, ..., b. From each of these marks, vertical line segments rise upward to meet the curve at P_0, P_1, P_2, ... P_(i minus 1), P_i, ..., and P_n, respectively. Slanted line segments connect P_0 to P_1, P_1 to P_2, and so on until P_n.

subsection.paragraph: The length $$L$$ of $$C$$ is approximately the length of this polygonal path and the approximation gets better as we let $$n$$ increase. (See Figure 4, where the arc of the curve between $$P_{i - 1}$$ and $$P_{i}$$ has been magnified and approximations with successively smaller values of $$\Delta x$$ are shown.) Therefore we define the length $$L$$ of the curve $$C$$ with equation $$y = f(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ , as the limit of the lengths of these approximating polygonal paths (if the limit exists):
where $$\left| P_{i - 1}P_{i} \right|$$ is the distance between the points $$P_{i - 1}$$ and $$P_{i}$$ .

subsection.paragraph: Notice that the procedure for defining arc length is very similar to the procedure we used for defining area and volume: We divided the curve into a large number of small parts. We then found the approximate lengths of the small parts and added them. Finally, we took the limit as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ .

The definition of arc length given by Equation 1 is not very convenient for computational purposes, but we can derive an integral formula for $$L$$ in the case where $$f$$ has a continuous derivative. [Such a function $$f$$ is called smooth because a small change in $$x$$ produces a small change in $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ .]
